note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: How many children worldwide are in child labour?
questions.whyCorrect: 138 million children — and 54 million of them do hazardous work that endangers their health or safety.
questions.action: Look up what counts as hazardous work for a child.

questions.prompt: How many children have been removed from child labour since 2000?
questions.whyCorrect: Over 100 million fewer children are working than in 2000 — one of the great untold successes, even though 138 million remain.
questions.action: Ask what got 100 million children out of work and into school.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's workers have informal jobs — no contract, no protection?
questions.whyCorrect: 57.8% — well over half the world's workers. No sick pay, no pension, no protection if they're dismissed.
questions.action: Ask what a work contract actually guarantees you.

questions.prompt: In sub-Saharan Africa and the least developed countries, informal work is about:
questions.whyCorrect: Nearly 90% of all workers. For women in least developed countries it's 93.8%, against 86.4% for men.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic for these regions.
questions.action: Compare 90% regionally with 57.8% globally.

questions.prompt: Global unemployment in 2024 hit what level?
questions.whyCorrect: A record low of 5.0%, down from 6.0% in 2015. Surprising to most people — but 57.8% of those jobs are informal.
whyWrong: Unemployment fell to a record low.
questions.action: Ask whether low unemployment means good jobs.

questions.prompt: How many young people are not in education, employment or training?
questions.whyCorrect: 259 million — about one in five young people worldwide are doing none of the three.
questions.action: Ask what happens to a young person's future in that situation.

questions.prompt: In Central and Southern Asia, young women not in work or education is 41.9%. For young men it's:
questions.whyCorrect: 11.5% — young women are nearly four times as likely to be excluded from both work and education in that region.
whyWrong: The gender gap is enormous, not small.
Young men fare far better than this.
questions.action: Ask what explains a 30-point gender gap.

questions.prompt: Youth unemployment is 12.9%. Adult unemployment is:
questions.whyCorrect: 3.7% — young people are about three and a half times more likely to be unemployed than adults.
questions.action: Ask why a first job is the hardest to get.

questions.prompt: Ending child labour by 2025 would need progress to speed up by how much?
questions.whyCorrect: An 11-fold acceleration. Between 2020 and 2024 the world moved 22 million children out of labour — impressive, and nowhere near enough.
whyWrong: The required acceleration is far larger.
questions.action: Ask what an 11x acceleration would actually require.

questions.prompt: Workers' rights protections between 2015 and 2023 got:
questions.whyCorrect: Compliance with labour rights deteriorated 7% globally — and 45.5% in the least developed countries. Rights are going backwards.
whyWrong: The trend is negative, not positive.
questions.action: Ask what labour rights protect a worker from.

questions.prompt: In the least developed countries, labour rights compliance fell by:
questions.whyCorrect: 45.5% — a collapse, and far worse than the 16.5% decline in developed economies. Rights eroded most where they were weakest already.
questions.action: Compare 45.5% with the developed-economy figure of 16.5%.

questions.prompt: How many children do hazardous work — jobs that can injure or kill them?
questions.whyCorrect: 54 million of the 138 million children in child labour — mining, heavy machinery, chemicals, long hours.
questions.action: Ask what makes work 'hazardous' rather than just hard.

questions.prompt: Least developed countries are meant to grow at 7% a year. Actual 2024 growth was:
questions.whyCorrect: 3.1% — under half the target, and falling from 4.7% in 2022 and 3.5% in 2023. Growth is slowing where it's needed most.
whyWrong: Above the target, which wasn't achieved.
questions.action: Ask why growth targets exist for poorer countries.

questions.prompt: Global income per person grew about how fast in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: Around 2% a year between 2022 and 2024, slowing to a projected 1.5% in 2025 amid trade tensions and uncertainty.
whyWrong: Far above actual global growth rates.
questions.action: Ask what 2% growth means for a family's income.

questions.prompt: In least developed countries, what share of working women are in informal jobs?
questions.whyCorrect: 93.8% — against 86.4% of men. Almost every working woman in the poorest countries works without protection.
questions.action: Ask what happens to an informal worker who gets sick.

questions.prompt: Tourism contributes what share of global GDP?
questions.whyCorrect: 3.4% of world GDP and 5.6% of global employment — bigger as a job creator than as an economic share.
questions.action: Ask how many people you know work in tourism.

questions.prompt: For Small Island Developing States, tourism is what share of GDP?
questions.whyCorrect: 13% of GDP and 12.9% of employment — nearly four times the global average. Island economies depend on visitors.
whyWrong: That's closer to the global average.
Too high, though dependence is real.
questions.action: Ask what happens to an island economy when tourism stops.

questions.prompt: Global unemployment fell from 6.0% in 2015 to 5.0%. Is that the whole story?
questions.whyCorrect: Record-low unemployment sits alongside 57.8% informal employment. Having a job and having a secure, protected job are different things.
whyWrong: Most of the world's work is informal and unprotected.
Unemployment genuinely fell to a record low.
questions.action: Ask what your ideal job would guarantee you.

questions.prompt: How much did child labour fall between 2020 and 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 22 million children left child labour in four years — real progress, though 11 times faster is needed to hit the target.
questions.action: Ask what happens to a child who stops working.

questions.prompt: Labour productivity growth in 2024 was:
questions.whyCorrect: 1.5%, down from a 1.8% average in 2015–2019. Workers producing more per hour is what makes wages rise, so slowing productivity matters.
whyWrong: It grew, though more slowly than before.
questions.action: Ask what makes a worker more productive.

questions.prompt: Which region had NEGATIVE productivity growth between 2015 and 2019?
options: Latin America and the Caribbean at -1.1%
questions.whyCorrect: Latin America and the Caribbean at -1.1% — workers producing less per hour than before, which makes rising wages nearly impossible.
whyWrong: Central and Southern Asia exceeded 3% in 2024.
questions.action: Ask what causes productivity to fall.

questions.prompt: Which region had the fastest productivity growth recently?
questions.whyCorrect: Eastern and South-Eastern Asia averaged 3.2% between 2020 and 2024 — roughly double the global rate.
whyWrong: Not identified as the fastest-growing region here.
Latin America saw negative growth in 2015–2019.
questions.action: Ask what that region did differently.

questions.prompt: One in five young people is not in education, work or training. Is that improving?
questions.whyCorrect: A 0.9 percentage-point fall in nine years. Essentially stagnant, leaving 259 million young people disconnected.
whyWrong: It improved slightly rather than worsening.
questions.action: Ask what would reconnect a young person to work or study.

questions.prompt: Tourism provides what share of global employment?
questions.whyCorrect: 5.6% of all jobs worldwide — more than its 3.4% share of GDP, because tourism is labour-intensive.
questions.action: Ask why tourism creates more jobs per dollar than some industries.

questions.prompt: Least developed countries' growth has moved which way since 2022?
questions.whyCorrect: Falling — 4.7% in 2022, 3.5% in 2023, 3.1% in 2024. The gap to the 7% target is widening rather than closing.
whyWrong: There has been a clear decline.
questions.action: Ask what slows growth in the poorest countries.

questions.prompt: What does 'informal employment' actually mean?
options: Work with no contract, protection or benefits
Work with a casual dress code
questions.whyCorrect: No contract, no sick pay, no pension, no legal protection — 57.8% of the world's workers, and nearly 90% in the poorest countries.
whyWrong: Informal work can be full-time; the issue is protection.
questions.action: List what you'd lose without a contract.

questions.prompt: Global GDP per person growth is projected to slow in 2025 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 1.5%, down from around 2% — slowed by trade tensions and policy uncertainty.
whyWrong: Far above any recent global rate.
questions.action: Ask how trade disputes reach ordinary households.

questions.prompt: Which is bigger: youth unemployment or adult unemployment?
questions.whyCorrect: Youth unemployment is about 3.5 times the adult rate — a consistent pattern almost everywhere in the world.
questions.action: Ask what makes employers hesitant to hire first-timers.

questions.prompt: Informal employment is projected to change by 2026 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 57.7%, down a tenth of a percentage point from 57.8%. Informality is one of the most stubborn features of the global economy.
questions.action: Ask why informality is so hard to shift.

questions.prompt: Which group is most likely to be in informal work?
options: Women in least developed countries at 93.8%
questions.whyCorrect: 93.8% of working women in least developed countries — the highest informality rate of any group measured.
whyWrong: European youth face unemployment, but not this informality rate.
Developed economies have far lower informality.
questions.action: Ask why women are more often in informal work.

questions.prompt: Child labour fell over 100 million since 2000. What does that prove?
options: It's solvable — the number responds to policy
questions.whyCorrect: A drop of over 100 million shows child labour responds to schooling, family income and enforcement. The remaining 138 million is a choice, not a fate.
whyWrong: Over 100 million children were removed from labour.
The trend has been downward for two decades.
questions.action: Ask which policies got children out of work.

questions.prompt: Labour rights declined 16.5% in developed economies. What does that show?
options: Rights are eroding even in rich countries
questions.whyCorrect: Even wealthy economies saw a 16.5% deterioration — though far less than the 45.5% collapse in least developed countries.
whyWrong: Developed economies saw measurable decline too.
questions.action: Ask what workplace rights exist where you live.

questions.prompt: For Small Island Developing States, tourism employment is:
questions.whyCorrect: 12.9% of all employment — more than one job in eight, against 5.6% globally.
whyWrong: Too high, though dependence is substantial.
questions.action: Ask what a hurricane does to an island's job market.

questions.prompt: Global unemployment at 5.0% is a record low. What's the catch?
options: Most jobs are informal and unprotected
questions.whyCorrect: Being employed says nothing about job quality. With 57.8% informality and labour rights declining 7%, the world has more jobs and worse protection.
whyWrong: Informality and rights erosion are serious caveats.
It genuinely fell to a record low.
questions.action: Ask what makes a job 'decent' rather than just a job.

questions.prompt: Latin America's tourism contribution to GDP is about:
questions.whyCorrect: 4.3% — above the global 3.4%, but far below Small Island Developing States at 13%.
questions.action: Rank three regions by tourism dependence.

questions.prompt: Central and Southern Asia's tourism GDP share is:
questions.whyCorrect: 2.2% — below the global average of 3.4%, and far below island economies.
questions.action: Ask what else drives this region's economy.

questions.prompt: Productivity growth slowed from 1.8% to 1.5%. Why does that matter for workers?
options: Wages rise when workers produce more per hour
It has no effect on pay
questions.whyCorrect: Productivity growth is what makes rising wages sustainable. When it slows, pay rises get harder to fund without inflation.
whyWrong: Productivity and wages are closely linked over time.
The relationship runs the other way.
questions.action: Ask what tools make your work faster.

questions.prompt: 138 million children work. Where does most child labour happen?
options: Often in agriculture and family enterprises
questions.whyCorrect: Most child labour is in agriculture and family-run work rather than the factories people picture — which makes it harder to see and regulate.
whyWrong: Factory child labour is a minority of cases.
questions.action: Ask why hidden work is harder to stop.

questions.prompt: Which target is Goal 8 furthest from?
questions.whyCorrect: Child labour needs an 11-fold acceleration to hit its target. Unemployment hit a record low and economies are growing, if slowly.
whyWrong: Unemployment fell to a record low of 5.0%.
Global GDP per capita is growing about 2%.
questions.action: Ask what an 11x acceleration means in practice.

questions.prompt: 259 million young people are disconnected from work and study. As a share that's:
questions.whyCorrect: About 20% — one young person in five worldwide is in neither education, employment nor training.
questions.action: Picture 20 young people. Four are in this position.

questions.prompt: Least developed countries need 7% growth. They're achieving:
questions.whyCorrect: 3.1% against a 7% target — under half, and falling year on year.
whyWrong: Growth is well below the target.
questions.action: Ask what 7% growth would change over a decade.

questions.prompt: In least developed countries, informal work for men is:
questions.whyCorrect: 86.4% — high, though still below women's 93.8%. Informality dominates work for both sexes in the poorest countries.
questions.action: Compare 86.4% and 93.8%. Why the gap?

questions.prompt: What makes youth unemployment different from adult unemployment?
options: Young people lack experience employers ask for
There are no youth jobs anywhere
questions.whyCorrect: At 12.9% against 3.7%, the youth rate reflects the experience paradox — you need a job to get experience and experience to get a job.
whyWrong: 259 million are disconnected, but unemployment measures active jobseekers.
Youth employment exists but is harder to access.
questions.action: Ask how someone gets their very first job.

questions.prompt: Global labour rights compliance declined 7%. Over what period?
questions.whyCorrect: Eight years, from 2015 to 2023 — the same period the SDGs have been running.
whyWrong: The decline was measured over eight years.
questions.action: Ask what changed for workers since 2015.

questions.prompt: Which of these improved most clearly since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: Unemployment fell a full percentage point to a record low. Labour rights declined 7% and informality barely moved.
whyWrong: It's projected to stay at about 57.7%.
questions.action: Ask why job quantity improved while quality didn't.

questions.prompt: Tourism is 3.4% of GDP but 5.6% of jobs. What does that tell you?
options: It employs a lot of people per dollar earned
questions.whyCorrect: Tourism is labour-intensive — hotels, guides, restaurants and transport need people. That's why it matters so much for employment in island economies.
whyWrong: It's one of the least automated major sectors.
Its job share exceeds its GDP share.
questions.action: List five jobs that exist because of tourists.

questions.prompt: How many children are in child labour but NOT hazardous work?
questions.whyCorrect: 138 million total minus 54 million in hazardous work leaves about 84 million — still work that keeps them out of school.
whyWrong: The majority are in non-hazardous child labour.
questions.action: Do the subtraction yourself: 138 minus 54.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the global jobs picture?
options: More jobs, but most without protection
questions.whyCorrect: Record-low unemployment at 5.0% alongside 57.8% informality and a 7% decline in labour rights. Quantity up, quality down.
whyWrong: Labour rights and informality both worsened.
Unemployment fell to a record low.
questions.action: Ask which matters more: having work, or having good work.

questions.prompt: In Central and Southern Asia, what share of young women are not in work or education?
questions.whyCorrect: 41.9% — more than two in five young women, against 11.5% of young men in the same region.
questions.action: Ask what would change that 30-point gap.

questions.prompt: What's the most surprising fact in Goal 8?
options: Unemployment is at a record high
Unemployment is at a record low while most work is informal
questions.whyCorrect: 5.0% unemployment — the best on record — alongside 57.8% of workers having no contract or protection. The headline number hides the real story.
whyWrong: It fell to a record low of 5.0%.
It fell from 160 million to 138 million since 2020.
questions.action: Ask what statistic you'd want instead of unemployment.
